Known as the 'rod-pushing' sport, Insuknawr is an indigenous game of Mizoram played exclusively by men. Participants use an 8-foot-long wooden rod and attempt to push their opponent out of a circle with a diameter of 16 to 18 feet. The game tests strength and stamina and has been declared the 'Mizo National Game' by the Mizoram State Sports Council.

A traditional combat-wrestling game played within a circle of about 16 feet in diameter on carpet grass. Participants aim to lift their opponent off the ground using strength, skill, and rapid movements of arms and legs. Kicking, stepping outside the ring, and bending knees are prohibited.
In this game, two individuals sit on a pole and balance themselves while attempting to strike each other with padded clubs. The objective is to maintain balance while displacing the opponent.
A traditional tug-of-war game where two teams pull on opposite ends of a rope, each trying to drag the other team across a central line. It emphasizes strength and teamwork.
A pre-Christian custom revived during the Chapchar Kut festival, where participants stuff boiled eggs into each other's mouths. It is a playful activity reflecting traditional Mizo hospitality.

Performed during the Chapchar Kut festival, this dance involves boys and girls standing in a circle alternately with their hands on each other's shoulders. Musicians stand inside the circle, playing rhythms to which participants dance.

A dance performed by a single person of either gender, accompanied by a group sitting in a circle clapping and musicians playing drums. The dancer performs until tired, then tags another to continue. The accompanying song, 'Chheih hla,' recounts heroic deeds and escapades.

Known as the 'guest dance,' traditionally performed by men. It was performed by honored invitees while entering the arena of a feast called 'khuangchawi.' Dancers move in the village streets wearing 'puandum' (traditional shawls).

Originating from the Pawi and Lakher communities, this dance was associated with war. After a raid or battle, a ceremony was performed to deride the vanquished. The dance relies solely on rhythm from gongs, cymbals, and drums, with participants standing in a circle.

Also known as the bamboo dance, it involves male performers holding pairs of bamboo staves on the ground. Female dancers step in and out between the beating bamboo staves in intricate steps. It is one of the most famous dances among Mizo communities.

A traditional folk wrestling style and a significant sport among the Naga tribes. Wrestlers aim to throw their opponents to the ground, showcasing strength, technique, and balance. It is a prominent feature during festivals and cultural events.

A semi-contact combat sport originating from the Sümi Naga tribe. Characterized by participants using only the soles of their feet to kick and block, the objective is to make the opponent fall or step out of the designated ring. It was traditionally used to settle disputes without resorting to violence.

A two-player abstract strategy board game played by the Angami Naga tribe. Similar to Alquerque, players aim to capture all of the opponent's pieces by hopping over them. The game emphasizes strategic planning and foresight.

A traditional game played in Viswema village, where participants throw thin bamboo sticks called 'Opche' from a set distance. The team that throws the stick the farthest wins. An open competition is held annually in January.

An indigenous game of the Southern Angami villages, played solely by men. It involves physical activity and is performed during cultural festivals to promote brotherhood and develop physical strength.
Another traditional game of the Southern Angami, details of which are limited, but it is performed during cultural events and festivals.
Played by the Yimkhiungru tribe during the winter season after harvest. Men spin their tops, and opponents attempt to hit the spinning top with their own, showcasing precision and timing.
A traditional game where participants attempt to climb a vertically erected bamboo pole that has been greased with mustard oil or animal fat. The challenge tests strength, agility, and technique.

A traditional sport among certain Naga tribes, where trained cocks are pitted against each other in a controlled environment. It requires skill in training the birds and is often accompanied by cultural rituals.
A traditional card game from Odisha, played with circular Pattachitra-painted cards. Originating in the 16th century, it involves various suits and is popular in regions like Puri and Ganjam.
A traditional game where participants squat and shift their weight from one leg to another in quick succession. It is commonly played by girls during festivals like Raja and Kumar Purnima.
A strategic board game representing a tiger and goats, where one player controls the tiger and the other controls multiple goats. The objective is for the goats to block the tiger's movements.
Also known as hopscotch, players draw a grid on the ground and take turns hopping on one foot to reach the end without stepping on the lines. It is a popular game among children.
A traditional board game played with small stones or seeds, involving strategic movement and capturing of the opponent's pieces.
A game that simulates daily activities, where children mimic fetching water from a pond or river and preparing traditional food items symbolically.
A traditional game where one player acts as a bride, and others attempt to 'steal' her without being caught by the 'groom' or 'family' members.
Played during the Raja festival, this game involves swinging on makeshift swings, often tied to trees, celebrating womanhood and the onset of monsoon.

Similar to Gilli Danda, this game involves a small stick (guchi) and a larger stick (tandu). The player uses the tandu to strike the guchi, flipping it into the air, and then hits it again to send it as far as possible.
A game where a handkerchief is placed in the center, and teams compete to retrieve it without being tagged by the opposing team.
A traditional game similar to blind man's buff, where one player is blindfolded and tries to catch the other players.

A game representing the collection of Mahua flowers, reflecting the day-to-day work of forest-dwelling tribal people in Western Odisha.

A role-playing game involving four players assigned roles of king, minister, thief, and police; the king tries to identify the thief based on the minister's hint.
A game where one player is blindfolded and tries to catch the other players. Once caught, the next player is blindfolded.

Also known as tug-of-war, this game involves two teams pulling on opposite ends of a rope, with the goal to bring the rope a certain distance in one direction against the force of the opposing team's pull.
A traditional game involving the throwing of coconuts, testing strength and accuracy.
A traditional game played in Odisha, details of which are limited but known to be part of the region's cultural heritage.

A contact team sport where players take turns to raid the opposing team's half, aiming to tag as many defenders as possible and return to their half without being tackled. It is a popular traditional sport in Punjab.

An amateur sport played with a long stick (danda) and a small, oval-shaped piece of wood (gilli). The player strikes the gilli with the danda, flipping it into the air, and then hits it again to send it as far as possible. It is similar to cricket and is popular among rural youth in Punjab.

A traditional game where children sit in a circle, and one child walks around the circle holding a cloth, singing a rhyme. The child secretly drops the cloth behind another child, who must then pick it up and chase the first child, attempting to tag them before they can sit in the vacated spot.

A classic children's game where one player closes their eyes and counts while the others hide. After counting, the seeker tries to find the hidden players. It is a popular game among both boys and girls in Punjab.

A game involving two teams. One team stacks seven flat stones and tries to knock them over with a ball. After knocking them over, the team attempts to rebuild the stack while the opposing team tries to hit them with the ball to prevent them from succeeding.

A game primarily played by girls, where two players clasp hands and spin in circles, singing traditional songs. It is a form of recreational activity and dance, reflecting the cultural heritage of Punjab.

Also known as hopscotch, this game involves drawing a grid on the ground and numbering the sections. Players throw a small object into the numbered sections and hop through the grid to retrieve it, following specific rules.

A traditional game where two teams pull on opposite ends of a rope, each trying to drag the other team across a central line. It tests strength and teamwork and is popular during festivals and fairs in Punjab.
A game involving a ball, where girls sing rhymes while playing. It is suitable for children and involves various rounds, each with its own song and actions.

A game played with pebbles or broken pieces of earthenware. Players sit on the floor and engage in activities involving these small objects, following specific rules. It is a traditional game that does not involve running or jumping.
A game for both boys and girls, generally played by two teams. It involves drawing as many vertical lines as possible, following specific rules and strategies.

A game played by boys, involving digging a pole into the ground and attaching a four-foot rope. Players place their shoes near the pole, and one player (the key player) tries to prevent others from retrieving their shoes by touching them.
Similar to field hockey, this game involves using a ball made of rags and a stick with a natural curve at one end. It is a traditional sport reflecting the rural culture of Punjab.

A game played by multiple players who dig holes in the ground, each representing a 'khuti' (peg). A larger central hole represents 'Rabb di Khuti' (God's peg). Players throw a ball into the air and engage in activities involving these holes, following specific rules.

A contact team sport where players take turns to raid the opposing team's half, aiming to tag as many defenders as possible and return to their half without being tackled. It is a popular traditional sport in Punjab.
Traditional wrestling arenas where boys learn wrestling from a Guru or Pehlwan (wrestler). These were popular in villages and often located near wells or temples.

A traditional form of martial arts practiced in Punjab, involving the use of weapons like sticks, swords, and shields. It is performed during religious and cultural festivals, showcasing skill and agility.
A popular activity in both urban and rural areas of Punjab, involving flying kites made of paper and bamboo. It is especially prominent during festivals like Basant Panchami.
A game played mostly by boys, involving spinning a wooden top (lattoo) using a string. The objective is to keep the top spinning for as long as possible.
A game involving small glass or stone marbles, where players aim to hit a target marble out of a designated area. It is popular among children in Punjab.

Also known as 'Dog and the Bone,' this traditional game involves two teams. A handkerchief (rumal) is placed in the center, and one player from each team attempts to grab it and return to their side without being tagged by the opponent. It emphasizes agility and strategy.

Known elsewhere as 'Lagori' or 'Seven Stones,' this game involves stacking seven flat stones and attempting to knock them over by throwing a ball. Players then try to rebuild the stack while the opposing team tries to prevent them by hitting them with the ball. It is popular in rural Rajasthan.

An ancient board game believed to have originated in India, Chaupar is played on a cross-shaped board with four arms. Each player has four pieces that they move based on the roll of cowrie shells. A traditional sport played with two sticks: a small one called 'gilli' and a larger one called 'danda.' The player uses the danda to strike the gilli, flipping it into the air, and then hits it again to send it flying. The aim is to hit the gilli as far as possible. It is reminiscent of cricket and is popular in rural Rajasthan.

A contact team sport where two teams take turns sending a 'raider' into the opposing team's half to tag as many defenders as possible and return to their own half without being tackled. The raider must chant 'kabaddi' continuously during the attempt. It is widely played in Rajasthan and has deep cultural roots.

A traditional tag game where two teams compete; one team sits or kneels in the middle of the field, and the other team runs around them. The objective is to tag the runners in the shortest time possible. It is a popular game in Rajasthan, especially in rural areas.

Similar to Satoliya, Pithoo involves stacking flat stones and attempting to knock them over with a ball. Players then try to rebuild the stack while avoiding being hit by the ball thrown by the opposing team. It is a common game among children in Rajasthan.

Traditional archery practiced in Rajasthan, reflecting the martial heritage of the region. Archery competitions are held during festivals and fairs, showcasing skill and precision.
A unique variation of polo played on camel-back, reflecting Rajasthan's desert culture. It was once a favorite sport of the Raja-Maharajas and is still showcased during cultural festivals.

Archery is deeply rooted in Sikkimese tradition and is especially popular among the Lepcha tribe. Competitions are often held during festivals like Losar (Tibetan New Year), and archery remains a beloved sport that requires precision and skill.

Sho is a traditional race game in Sikkim, originating from Tibet. The name 'Sho' means 'dice' in Tibetan. It is traditionally played for money by men, with two to four players, three being the most common. With four players, the usual variant is to play as two teams of two, with the partners sitting opposite each other.

Kavadi is a traditional toy resembling a catapult, made from bamboo. It consists of a curved bamboo strip with a rubber band tied at one end. Children place small stones or other lightweight objects on the curved strip, pull the rubber band, and release it to send the objects flying. It is a popular toy among children in Sikkim.

Cop Khel is a traditional game played using a board with carved squares and stones as game pieces. The objective is to capture the opponent's stones by strategically moving one's own pieces. This game enhances cognitive skills, problem-solving, and critical thinking abilities.

Pipo is a traditional game that requires skill and agility. It involves bouncing a small rubber ball with a curved wooden bat. The objective is to keep the ball in the air for as long as possible by hitting it with the bat, improving hand-eye coordination, concentration, and reflexes.

A traditional martial art involving the use of a bamboo staff, focusing on self-defense techniques, agility, and flexibility. It has been practiced since the Sangam period and remains integral to Tamil culture.
A traditional mancala board game played with a wooden board featuring fourteen pits and 146 shells. It is popular among women and children, enhancing mathematical skills and strategic thinking.

Also known as 'Lambs and Tigers,' this strategic board game involves two teams: one controlling three tigers and the other controlling up to fifteen lambs. The objective is for the tigers to hunt the lambs while the lambs aim to block the tigers' movements.

A traditional bull-taming sport practiced during the Pongal festival, where participants attempt to embrace and hold onto a bull's hump as it tries to escape. It has been a part of Tamil culture since the Sangam period.
A festive game where participants, often blindfolded, attempt to break a suspended earthen pot using a stick. It is commonly played during Krishna Janmashtami celebrations.

A traditional dice game played with long cuboid dice and coins. Players roll the dice to move their coins around a cross-shaped board, aiming to bring all their coins to the center before their opponents.
A hopping game where players draw a grid on the ground and hop on one leg to complete the course without stepping on the lines. It enhances balance and coordination.

An indoor board game played by 2-4 players, where each aims to bring all six of their coins home before the opponents. Players use cowries as dice to move their coins along the board, with opportunities to cut each other's coins to race ahead.

Also known as cockfighting, this traditional rural sport involves roosters with blades attached to their feet fighting each other. It has historical significance in Tamil culture but has faced modern scrutiny due to animal welfare concerns.
A traditional bullock cart racing sport where participants race their decorated carts, typically during festivals. It showcases the agricultural heritage and competitive spirit of rural Tamil Nadu.

A traditional game requiring quick reflexes and team effort. One player, called the 'kili' (parrot), stands in the center, while others move horizontally. The objective is to capture the 'kili' by coordinating movements.
A traditional sport where participants lift huge spherical rocks, testing their strength and endurance. It is often showcased during village festivals and gatherings.

A game involving spinning tops, where players launch their tops using a string and attempt to keep them spinning the longest or knock other tops out of a designated area. It enhances hand-eye coordination.

A game resembling cricket and baseball, played with two sticks: a 'gilli' (small stick) and a 'danda' (longer stick). The player strikes the gilli with the danda, flipping it into the air, and then hits it again to cover maximum distance.

A traditional tag sport where teams take turns chasing and evading, with players sitting in a row and active chasers running around them. It emphasizes speed, strategy, and teamwork.
A contact team sport where players take turns to raid the opposing team's half, aiming to tag opponents and return to their half without being tackled. It requires strength, strategy, and agility.
Known as 'Kallangal' or 'Anchangal' in Tamil Nadu, this game involves tossing and catching five small stones in various sequences. It enhances hand-eye coordination and concentration.
A game where players jump over a swinging rope, either individually or in groups, often accompanied by songs or rhymes. It improves cardiovascular fitness and rhythm.
An ancient board game believed to be the precursor to modern chess, involving strategic movement of pieces representing different military units on an 8x8 grid.

A traditional board game similar to Ludo, played with cowrie shells and a board divided into a cross pattern. Players race their four pieces from start to finish based on the count of the cowrie shells thrown. It is popular in Telugu-speaking regions, including Telangana.

Also known as Nine Men's Morris, this strategic board game involves two players who aim to form 'mills'—three of their pieces in a row—allowing them to remove an opponent's piece. The game continues until a player is reduced to two pieces. It has historical significance in Telangana.

Translating to 'Tiger and Goat Game,' this is a strategic two-player (or two-team) game where one side controls three tigers and the other controls up to 15 goats. The tigers attempt to 'hunt' the goats, while the goats aim to block the tigers' moves. It reflects the predator-prey dynamics and is popular in rural Telangana.

Also known as Pallanghuzi, this traditional mancala game is played on a wooden board with 14 pits. Players distribute seeds, shells, or stones across the pits, aiming to capture more than the opponent. It enhances mathematical skills and strategic thinking and is enjoyed in various parts of Telangana.

Known locally as Lingorcha, this game involves stacking seven flat stones and attempting to knock them over by throwing a ball. Once the pile is knocked over, the team must try to restore the stack while the opposing team throws the ball to hit the players. It tests agility and teamwork.

Translating to 'Game of Four Pillars,' this traditional game involves four players, each occupying one of four pillars. A fifth player stands in the center, attempting to tag the others as they dash between pillars. It was commonly played in traditional homes with central courtyards in Telangana.

Also known as Lagori, this game involves stacking seven stones and attempting to knock them over with a ball. Players then try to rebuild the stack while the opposing team tries to prevent them by hitting them with the ball. It is a popular game among children in Telangana.

An ancient Indian strategy board game believed to be a precursor to modern chess. Played on an 8x8 grid, it involves two armies with various pieces, each having specific movements. The objective is to capture the opponent's king. It has historical roots in the region.

A traditional hopscotch game where players draw a grid on the ground and toss a marker into numbered sections. They hop through the grid on one foot to retrieve the marker, avoiding lines and specific sections. It promotes balance and coordination and is popular among children in Telangana.

A traditional game involving a small stick ('karra') and a flat stone ('billa'). Players use the stick to strike the stone, flipping it into the air, and then hit it again to send it flying. The objective is to cover maximum distance. It is similar to Gilli Danda and is played in rural Telangana.

A traditional wrestling game played between two young men to test their strength. Players sit facing each other with legs spread and a bamboo pole placed between them. They hold a horizontal bamboo piece and attempt to pull it towards their side.

Similar to the game of gilli-danda, Tengdang is played with two tools: a stick called 'dang' and a smaller stick called 'goti'. Both are made from branches of trees. The objective is to strike the goti with the dang to send it as far as possible.

In this game, a small footstep is tied on two pieces of bamboo about two feet above ground level. The player walks on this footstep, competing to run faster or remain on the kaldong longer without falling.

A swinging game played by Tripuri children. Two long ropes or strong vines are tied to a tree branch, with a wooden platform as a seat. Children take turns swinging while others push and sing traditional songs.

A strength-testing game where a child clings to a man's chest, whose waist is tied with one end of a rope. Another man holds the other end and tries to pull the first man back, while the first man attempts to move forward.

A game to test grip strength. A cylindrical bamboo section is held firmly on the ground by one person, while another grips it above and tries to snatch it by rotating.

A traditional game similar to blind man's buff, popular in Tripura. One player is blindfolded and tries to catch others, who attempt to avoid being caught.

Known locally as Saz Loung, this traditional game involves drawing a large rectangular box on the ground, subdivided into six smaller boxes named Awal, Doum, Soum, Jaanat, Samandar, and Jehnum. Players hop through these boxes on one foot, aiming to retrieve a marker without stepping on the lines. It is popular among both boys and girls.

Also known as Santooli, this game involves stacking seven flat stones and attempting to knock them over by throwing a ball. Players then try to rebuild the stack while the opposing team tries to prevent them by hitting them with the ball. It is a common game among children in Kashmir.

Popularly known as Bante Zaar, this game involves playing with glass marbles. Players aim to hit a target marble or shoot marbles into a hole, requiring precision and strategic planning. It is a favorite pastime among Kashmiri children.
A traditional game played in Kashmir, though specific details about its gameplay are limited. It is one of the many games that were played with enthusiasm and had great cultural value.
A game similar to football, mostly played by boys in Kashmir. The ball used in this game is made out of old cloth or rug, reflecting the resourcefulness of the players.

In this game, one player is blindfolded using a piece of cloth, and the other players tease him or her by pushing, pulling clothes, and running around. The blindfolded player attempts to catch the others, adding an element of fun and excitement.
A traditional sport in Srinagar, where participants engage in wrestling matches, showcasing strength and skill. It is a significant part of local festivals and gatherings.

A traditional archery game played during festivals and special occasions in Srinagar. Archers, dressed in traditional attire called pheran, use bows and arrows made of bamboo and wood to shoot at targets, preserving the archery skills practiced in the region for centuries.

A unique sport played on the frozen lakes of Srinagar during winter months. Players ride on horseback and try to score goals by hitting a small ball with a mallet, reflecting the adaptation of traditional polo to snowy conditions.
Also known as Tug of War, this traditional game involves two teams pulling on opposite ends of a rope, each trying to drag the other across a designated line. It promotes teamwork and strength.

A traditional board game popular among locals in Srinagar. Played on a wooden board with pits and seeds or stones, the objective is to capture the opponent's pieces by strategically moving them around the board.

A traditional sport deeply ingrained in Ladakhi culture, often played during summer festivals. Villages host archery competitions accompanied by traditional music, dancing, and festivities. Participants aim at targets with bows and arrows, showcasing their precision and skill.

Introduced in the mid-17th century, polo has become a significant traditional sport in Ladakh. Played with teams of six, the game involves scoring goals by hitting a ball into the opposing team's net using long-handled mallets while riding horses. It remains a popular event during local festivals.

A unique and exhilarating sport where participants race yaks over a designated course. Often held during traditional festivals, these races are accompanied by dances and songs, reflecting the rich cultural heritage of the region.

Emerging as a popular winter sport in Ladakh, ice hockey is played on natural ice surfaces from mid-December to mid-February. The region has produced national-level players, with local tournaments drawing significant attention.

During the Dosmoche festival, various traditional games and mask dances are performed to ward off evil spirits and ensure prosperity. These festivities include ritualistic dances, traditional music, and communal activities that strengthen social bonds.

A French game introduced during colonial times, Pétanque involves players throwing metal balls aiming to land as close as possible to a smaller wooden ball called a 'cochonnet'. It remains popular in Puducherry, especially among the older Franco-Indian community.
An ancient martial art form native to South India, Silambam is practiced in Puducherry. It involves the use of a bamboo staff for self-defense and showcases agility, balance, and coordination.

A traditional Indian tag game where two teams compete; one team sits or kneels in a row, and the opposing team's runners try to avoid being touched by members of the sitting team. It emphasizes speed, strategy, and teamwork. Played in Puducherry's schools and communities.

A contact team sport where players take turns to raid the opposing team's half, aiming to tag opponents and return to their half without being tackled. It requires strength, strategy, and agility. Popular in various parts of Puducherry.

A tabletop game originating from the Indian subcontinent, Carrom is very popular in Puducherry. Players use a striker disk with a flick of the finger to move lighter object discs into one of four corner pockets.
A traditional game where players use a shooter marble to hit target marbles out of a designated area. It requires precision and strategy and is commonly played by children in Puducherry.

A game involving spinning a wooden top using a string. Players compete to see whose top spins the longest or to knock other tops out of a designated area. It is a popular traditional game among children in Puducherry.

A traditional game where players stack seven flat stones and attempt to knock them over with a ball. After knocking the stones, the team tries to restore the pile while the opposing team throws the ball to hit them. It is a favorite pastime in Puducherry.

Telugu is the official and most widely spoken language in Andhra Pradesh, belonging to the Dravidian language family. It has a rich literary tradition and is recognized as one of India's classical languages.
Urdu is spoken by a minority in Andhra Pradesh, primarily among the Muslim community. It has historical significance due to the Nizam's rule in the region.
Gondi is a Dravidian language spoken by the Gond tribe in parts of Andhra Pradesh. It is considered vulnerable due to declining usage among younger generations.
Kolami is another Dravidian language spoken by tribal communities in Andhra Pradesh. It has several dialects and is primarily used in rural areas.
Kuvi is spoken by the Khond tribe in the hilly regions of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. It is known for its unique phonetic and grammatical structures.
Also known as Banjara, Lambadi is spoken by the Banjara community in Andhra Pradesh. It has influences from various languages due to the nomadic history of its speakers.
Koya is a Dravidian language spoken by the Koya tribe in the border areas of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Chhattisgarh. It is used in daily communication and cultural practices.
Chenchu is spoken by the Chenchu tribe, primarily residing in the Nallamala forest region of Andhra Pradesh. It is an endangered language with limited documentation.
Yerukala, also known as Erukala, is spoken by the Yerukala tribe in Andhra Pradesh. It is part of the Dravidian language family and has distinct linguistic features.
Savara is a Munda language spoken by the Sora tribe in parts of Andhra Pradesh. It has its own script and a rich oral tradition.
Konda is a Dravidian language spoken by the Konda-Dora tribe in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh. It is considered endangered due to a decreasing number of speakers.
Manda is a lesser-known Dravidian language spoken by a small tribal community in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. It is critically endangered with very few speakers remaining.
Ollari is a Dravidian language spoken by tribal groups in the border areas of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. It is closely related to the Gondi language.
Naiki, also known as Naiki-Gondi, is a Dravidian language spoken by certain tribal communities in Andhra Pradesh. It serves as a link between Gondi and other related languages.
Pattapu is a Dravidian language spoken by a small community in Andhra Pradesh. It is one of the lesser-documented languages in the region.
Spoken by the Nyishi tribe, this language belongs to the Tani group within the Sino-Tibetan family. It is one of the most widely spoken indigenous languages in Arunachal Pradesh.
The Adi language is used by the Adi people and comprises several dialects, including Minyong, Padam, and Pasi. It is part of the Tani branch and is prevalent in central Arunachal Pradesh.
Spoken by the Apatani tribe in the Ziro valley, this language is unique within the Tani group and has distinct phonological features.
The Galo language is used by the Galo tribe and is part of the Tani subgroup. It has several dialects and is spoken in the western part of the state.
Spoken by the Tagin tribe, this language is another member of the Tani group and is found in the Upper Subansiri district.
Also known as Plains Miri, this language is spoken by the Mishing people residing along the Assam-Arunachal border. It is closely related to the Adi language.
Used by the Idu Mishmi tribe, this language is part of the Mishmic group and is spoken in the Dibang Valley. It is considered endangered due to declining usage among younger generations.
Also known as Taraon, this language is spoken by the Digaro Mishmi people and is part of the Mishmic group. It is prevalent in the Lohit district.
Spoken by the Miju Mishmi tribe, this language belongs to the Mishmic group and is found in the eastern regions of Arunachal Pradesh.
The Monpa language encompasses several dialects spoken by the Monpa people in the Tawang and West Kameng districts. It is part of the Tibetic language family.
Used by the Sherdukpen community, this language is spoken in the West Kameng district and has influences from both Tibetic and indigenous languages.
Also known as Khowa, this language is spoken by the Bugun tribe in the West Kameng district. It is considered endangered due to a limited number of speakers.
Spoken by the Hruso (Aka) people, this language is found in the West Kameng district and is considered endangered.
Also known as Sajolang, this language is spoken by the Miji people in the West Kameng district. It has two main dialects: Western and Eastern Miji.
A recently documented language, Koro is spoken by a small community in the East Kameng district. Its classification within the Sino-Tibetan family remains uncertain.
The Nocte language is used by the Nocte tribe in the Tirap district. It is part of the Konyak subgroup of Naga languages.
Spoken by the Wancho tribe, this language is prevalent in the Longding district and is closely related to the Nocte language.
The Tangsa language comprises numerous dialects spoken by the Tangsa people in the Changlang district. It is part of the Northern Naga group.
Used by the Singpho tribe, this language is spoken in the eastern parts of Arunachal Pradesh and is closely related to the Jingpho language of Myanmar.
Spoken by the Chakma community, this language belongs to the Indo-Aryan family and is found in the southwestern regions of Arunachal Pradesh.
The Tai Khamti language is used by the Khamti people and is part of the Tai language family. It is spoken in the Lohit district and has its own script.
Also known as Sulung, this language is spoken by the Puroik people in various districts. It is considered endangered due to a small number of speakers.
Spoken by the Bangru community, this language is found in the Kurung Kumey district and is closely related to the Miji language.
Also known as Zakhring, this language is spoken by the Meyor people in the easternmost regions of Arunachal Pradesh. It is considered highly endangered.

The official language of Assam, Assamese is an Eastern Indo-Aryan language spoken by over 15 million people. It has various dialects, including Eastern, Central, Kamrupi, and Goalpariya, each reflecting regional nuances.
A Sino-Tibetan language primarily spoken in the Bodoland Territorial Region of Assam. Recognized as one of the 22 scheduled languages of India, Bodo has its own script and rich oral literature.

Belonging to the Tani branch of the Sino-Tibetan family, Mising is spoken by the Mising tribe residing along the Brahmaputra River. The language has been influenced by Assamese due to prolonged contact.
A member of the Sino-Tibetan family, Karbi is spoken by the Karbi tribe in the hilly regions of Assam. It features several dialects and is integral to the tribe's cultural identity.

Part of the Bodo-Garo group within the Sino-Tibetan family, Dimasa is spoken by the Dimasa community in Dima Hasao district. The language has its own script and a rich tradition of folk songs and tales.
A Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Rabha community in western Assam and parts of Meghalaya. It has multiple dialects and reflects the community's unique cultural heritage.
Also known as Lalung, Tiwa is a Tibeto-Burman language spoken by the Tiwa tribe in central Assam. The language is an essential aspect of Tiwa cultural practices and rituals.
Belonging to the Sino-Tibetan family, Deori is spoken by the Deori tribe in Assam. The language has retained many archaic features and is considered endangered.
A Tai-Kadai language that was historically spoken by the Ahom people who ruled Assam for six centuries. While no longer in everyday use, Ahom is preserved through religious chants and manuscripts.
A group of dialects spoken in the Goalpara region of Assam. These dialects have a mix of Assamese, Bengali, and local linguistic features, reflecting the area's diverse cultural interactions.
A western dialect of Assamese spoken in the Kamrup region. It has distinct phonetic and lexical features that set it apart from standard Assamese.
A Kukish language spoken by the Hmar people in parts of Assam, Manipur, and Mizoram. It has its own script and a rich tradition of folk literature.
An Indo-Aryan language spoken by the Hajong people in Assam and Meghalaya. It serves as a bridge between Assamese and Bengali, incorporating elements of both languages.
An Indo-Aryan language spoken by the Bishnupriya community in Assam and Manipur. It combines features of Bengali, Assamese, and Meitei, reflecting a unique cultural synthesis.
An extinct language that was once spoken by the Chutia people in Assam. Efforts are underway to revive the language through the study of historical documents and oral traditions.

An Indo-Aryan language spoken in the northern and eastern regions of Bihar, particularly in the historical Mithila region. Maithili has a rich literary tradition and is recognized under the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.
Predominantly spoken in the western parts of Bihar, Bhojpuri extends into eastern Uttar Pradesh and the Terai region of Nepal. It has several dialects and is known for its vibrant folk traditions.
Also known as Magadhi, this language is spoken in the central areas of Bihar, including districts like Patna, Gaya, and Nalanda. It is believed to be the descendant of the ancient Magadhi Prakrit.
Spoken in the Anga region, which includes districts like Bhagalpur and Munger in Bihar. Angika has a significant number of speakers and shares linguistic features with both Maithili and Magahi.
Also referred to as Western Maithili, Bajjika is spoken in the northwestern parts of Bihar, particularly in the Tirhut region encompassing districts like Muzaffarpur and Vaishali.
A language variety spoken in the Purnia division of Bihar, including districts like Araria, Purnia, Katihar, and Kishanganj. It shares linguistic features with Assamese and Bengali.
Spoken in the southern regions of Bihar, particularly in areas adjoining Jharkhand. Khortha is considered a dialect of Magahi and is prevalent among rural communities.
An Austroasiatic language spoken by the Santhal tribal community in parts of Bihar, especially in districts like Jamui, Banka, and Bhagalpur. Santali has its own script called Ol Chiki.

Also known as Panchpargania, this language is spoken by the Kurmi community in parts of southern Bihar and adjoining areas of Jharkhand. It is considered to have a close affinity with the Maithili language.
Spoken by the Tharu tribal community in the northern regions of Bihar, particularly in the Champaran districts. Tharu languages have influences from neighboring languages such as Awadhi and Maithili.

An Indo-Aryan language spoken by approximately 16.25 million people in Chhattisgarh and neighboring states. It is the official language of Chhattisgarh and is grouped within the Eastern Hindi languages.
A dialect of Chhattisgarhi spoken in the Surguja region. It is sometimes considered its own language due to its distinctiveness.
A Dravidian language spoken by the Gond tribes in southern Chhattisgarh, particularly in the Bastar region. Gondi has several dialects, including Muria and Madia.
A blend of Hindi, Odia, Marathi, and Chhattisgarhi, Halbi is spoken by tribal communities in eastern Bastar. It serves as a lingua franca among various tribes in the region.

A Dravidian language spoken by the Oraon tribe in the Surguja region. It is one of the indigenous languages of Chhattisgarh.

A dialect of Gondi spoken by the Muria tribe in north Bastar. It transitions into the Madia dialect further south.
A dialect of Gondi spoken by the Madia tribe in southern Bastar. It is closely related to the Muria dialect spoken in the northern parts of Bastar.
A dialect that is transitional between Gondi and Koya, spoken along the borders of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
A Dravidian language spoken by the Koya tribe along the borders of Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana. It shares similarities with Gondi and other regional languages.
A dialect of Gondi spoken by the Abujhmaria tribe in the Abujhmarh hills of Bastar. It is known for its unique linguistic features and relative isolation.
A Dravidian language spoken by the Dhurwa tribe in Bastar. It is closely related to Gondi and shares cultural significance with the tribal communities.
A language spoken by the Kamar tribe in the forested regions of Chhattisgarh. It is part of the Indo-Aryan language family and reflects the tribe's unique cultural identity.
A dialect spoken by the Baiga tribe in Chhattisgarh. It is considered a variant of Chhattisgarhi with distinct linguistic features.

The official language of Goa, Konkani is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by the majority of Goans. It has multiple dialects influenced by historical and cultural interactions, and is written in various scripts including Devanagari, Roman, Kannada, and Malayalam.

A central dialect of the Konkani macrolanguage, Goan Konkani is primarily spoken in the state of Goa. It includes sub-dialects such as Antruz, Bardeskari, and Saxtti, each reflecting unique regional and cultural nuances.

Introduced during the Portuguese colonial rule from 1510 to 1961, Portuguese was the official language of Goa. While its use has declined, it remains spoken among some older Goans and has left a lasting impact on Goan culture, architecture, and cuisine.

Developed during the colonial era, this creole language emerged from the interaction between Portuguese colonizers and native Konkani speakers. It incorporates elements of both languages and reflects the blending of cultures during that period.
Spoken by a significant minority in Goa, Marathi has historical ties to the region. It is used in education, media, and literature, and coexists with Konkani in various aspects of Goan society.

Due to historical interactions and migration, Kannada is spoken by a portion of Goa's population, particularly in areas bordering Karnataka. It has influenced certain Konkani dialects and contributes to the state's linguistic diversity.
Widely understood and spoken in Goa, Hindi is used in education, administration, and media. It serves as a lingua franca, facilitating communication among diverse linguistic communities in the state.

Serving as a global lingua franca, English is extensively used in Goa, especially in education, business, and tourism. Its widespread use enhances Goa's accessibility to international visitors and reflects its cosmopolitan character.
Spoken by a smaller segment of Goa's population, Urdu contributes to the state's linguistic mosaic. It is used in cultural and religious contexts, particularly within the Muslim community.

Within the Muslim communities of Goa, unique Konkani dialects have evolved, incorporating Arabic and Persian loanwords. These dialects reflect the cultural and religious influences specific to these communities.
An Indo-Aryan language and the official language of Gujarat, spoken by over 46 million people. It has multiple dialects and serves as the primary language for the majority of the state's population.
A dialect of Gujarati spoken in the Saurashtra region, also known as Kathiawar. It reflects the cultural and linguistic nuances of the area.
A dialect prevalent in the southern part of Gujarat, particularly around the city of Surat. It has distinct phonetic and lexical features.
Spoken in the Charotar region of central Gujarat, this dialect showcases unique linguistic characteristics influenced by the local culture.

A language spoken in the Kutch region, it has its own distinct identity but shares similarities with Sindhi and Gujarati. Kutchi is known for its rich oral traditions and is written using the Gujarati script.
A tribal language spoken by the Bhil community in parts of Gujarat. It is part of the Western Indo-Aryan language family and has several dialects within Gujarat.
A language spoken by the Rathwa tribe in Gujarat, reflecting the unique cultural and linguistic heritage of the community.
Spoken by certain tribal communities in Gujarat, Vasavi contributes to the state's linguistic diversity.

Spoken by the Dhodia tribe in Gujarat, this language reflects the tribe's distinct cultural identity.

Haryanvi is an Indo-Aryan language spoken primarily in the Indian state of Haryana and the territory of Delhi. It is considered part of the Western Hindi dialect group, which also includes Khariboli and Braj. Haryanvi is written in the Devanagari script.

Bangru, also known as Bangaru or Haryanvi, is the most widely spoken dialect in Haryana. It is prevalent in districts such as Rohtak, Sonipat, and Jhajjar, and is considered the standard form of Haryanvi.

Ahirwati is a dialect spoken by the Yadav community in regions including Rewari, Narnaul, and Mahendragarh. It is prevalent in the Ahirwal area and is the second most spoken dialect in the Haryanvi language.

Bagri is a dialect spoken in the western parts of Haryana, particularly in the Bagar region covering Sirsa, Fatehabad, and parts of Hisar and Bhiwani districts. It shares similarities with Rajasthani and Punjabi languages.
Mewati is spoken in the Mewat region, encompassing Nuh district, parts of Palwal, and Sohna in Haryana. It is closely related to Rajasthani and has its own distinct linguistic features.

Deswali, also known as Desari or Desaru, is spoken in the Deswal region covering districts of Rohtak, Sonipat, and Jhajjar. It is a dialect of Haryanvi with unique phonetic and lexical characteristics.
Jatu is a sub-dialect of Deswali, spoken by Jats and Rors in the low-lying khadir floodplains on the western banks of the Yamuna in Panipat, Karnal, Kurukshetra, and Yamunanagar districts.
Braj Bhasha is spoken in the southern districts of Haryana, including Faridabad and Palwal. It is an important dialect with historical significance in literature and poetry.
Puadhi is spoken in the northeastern districts of Haryana, such as Panchkula, Ambala, and parts of Kurukshetra. It shares linguistic features with Punjabi and Hindi.
Rangri is a dialect of Haryanvi used by Haryanvi-Muslim migrants living in Pakistan. It reflects the linguistic heritage of the Ranghar community.

Sansi is a distinct language spoken by the Sansi nomads in Haryana. It has influences from Rajasthani, Punjabi, Haryanvi, and Hindi languages, reflecting the diverse cultural interactions of the community.
Rathi is spoken in central Sirsa district and northern Fatehabad district. It is a dialect with unique linguistic features within the Haryanvi language spectrum.
Malwai is spoken in the northern Sirsa district, including areas like Mandi Dabwali, Kalanwali, and Odhan. It is also spoken in parts of Fatehabad district and shares features with Punjabi dialects.
Spoken primarily in the Kangra district, Kangri is a Western Pahari language. It shares linguistic features with neighboring dialects and reflects the cultural heritage of the Kangra region.
Native to the Mandi district, Mandeali is another Western Pahari language. It has several dialects and is integral to the local identity of the Mandi region.
Spoken in the Kullu Valley, Kullui is a dialect of the Western Pahari languages. It reflects the unique cultural and geographical characteristics of the Kullu region.
Associated with the Chamba district, Chambeali is a Western Pahari language. It has its own distinct linguistic features, setting it apart from neighboring dialects.
Also known as Kahluri, this dialect is spoken in the Bilaspur district. It is part of the Western Pahari group and reflects the local traditions of Bilaspur.
Predominantly spoken in the Shimla and Solan districts, Mahasu Pahari comprises several sub-dialects. It is an essential part of the cultural fabric of the Mahasu region.
Used in the Sirmaur district, Sirmauri is a dialect of the Western Pahari languages. It showcases the linguistic diversity within Himachal Pradesh.
Spoken by the inhabitants of the Pangi Valley in the Chamba district, Pangwali is a lesser-known dialect. It reflects the unique cultural identity of the Pangi region.

Spoken in the Kinnaur district, Kinnauri belongs to the West Himalayish branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family. It has several dialects and is integral to the cultural identity of the Kinnauri people.

Also known as Manchad, this language is spoken in the Lahaul region. It is part of the West Himalayish branch and is considered endangered due to a declining number of speakers.
Spoken exclusively in the Malana village of Kullu district, Kanashi is an isolated language with unique linguistic features. It is considered endangered due to its limited number of speakers.

An Austroasiatic language spoken by the Santal tribe, Santali is one of the prominent tribal languages in Jharkhand. It has its own script, Ol Chiki, and a rich tradition of oral literature, including folklore and songs.

Spoken by the Munda tribe, Mundari is an Austroasiatic language with a significant presence in Jharkhand. It shares linguistic features with other Munda languages and is integral to the cultural practices of the Munda people.
Another Austroasiatic language, Ho is spoken by the Ho tribe primarily in the West Singhbhum district. The language has its own script, Warang Citi, and a rich oral tradition.
A Dravidian language spoken by the Oraon tribe, Kurukh is prevalent in Jharkhand. Efforts have been made to preserve and promote the language through educational initiatives and literature.
An Indo-Aryan language, Khortha is widely spoken in the northern districts of Jharkhand. It serves as a lingua franca among various communities and has a rich collection of folk songs and stories.
Also known as Sadri, Nagpuri is an Indo-Aryan language spoken in the central region of Jharkhand. It has a significant body of folk literature and is used in local media and education.
Spoken by the Kudumi Mahato community, Kurmali is an Indo-Aryan language with roots in Jharkhand. It shares similarities with Bengali and Odia and is used in cultural and religious contexts.
An Austroasiatic language spoken by the Bhumij tribe, it is closely related to Mundari and shares cultural significance within the tribal communities of Jharkhand.

Belonging to the Austroasiatic family, Kharia is spoken by the Kharia tribe in Jharkhand. The language has distinct phonological and grammatical features and is used in daily communication and rituals.
A Dravidian language spoken by the Malto tribe, also known as Paharia, primarily in the Rajmahal hills. It is considered endangered, with efforts underway to document and revitalize it.
A highly endangered Munda language spoken by the Birhor tribe, known for their nomadic lifestyle. The language is at risk of extinction, with very few speakers remaining.
An Austroasiatic language spoken by the Asur tribe in Jharkhand. It is considered endangered, with efforts being made to preserve its oral traditions and promote its use among younger generations.

The official language of Karnataka, Kannada is a Dravidian language with a rich literary history dating back to the 9th century. It has several dialects influenced by various regions within the state.
A dialect of Kannada spoken predominantly in the Mysore and Bangalore regions. It is considered the standard form of Kannada and is widely used in education and media.
Spoken in the northern districts of Karnataka, particularly in Dharwad, this dialect has unique phonetic and lexical features distinguishing it from other Kannada dialects.

Also known as Kodava Takk, this language is spoken by the Kodava community in the Kodagu district. It has its own script and is notable for its unique syntactic and phonological characteristics.

A dialect spoken by the Beary Muslim community in the coastal districts. It is a mix of Tulu, Malayalam, and Arabic, reflecting the community's diverse cultural heritage.
A dialect used by the Havyaka Brahmin community, primarily in the Western Ghats region. It retains many archaic features of Kannada and has a distinct vocabulary.
Also known as Gowda Kannada, this dialect is spoken by the Gowda community in the Kodagu and Dakshina Kannada districts. It serves as a link between Kannada and Tulu.
A dialect spoken by the Sankethi community, who migrated from Tamil Nadu to Karnataka. It blends elements of Kannada, Tamil, and Sanskrit.
A Dravidian language spoken by the Badaga community in the Nilgiri Hills, straddling the border between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. It has its own script and a rich oral literature.
Spoken by the Lambani (Banjara) community, this language has roots in Rajasthani and has incorporated elements from Kannada and Telugu due to migration.
A Dravidian language spoken by the Koraga tribal community in the coastal districts. It is considered endangered due to the declining number of speakers.
The Siddi community, of African descent, resides in parts of Karnataka and speaks a dialect that is a blend of Konkani, Kannada, and their ancestral languages.
Spoken by the Irula tribal community in the southern regions of Karnataka and neighboring states. It is a Dravidian language with limited documentation.
A dialect spoken by the Holaya community in Karnataka. It is closely related to Kannada but has distinct phonetic and lexical features.
Spoken by the Sholaga tribal community in the southern parts of Karnataka. It is a Dravidian language with unique linguistic traits.

Used in the Wayanad district, this dialect has distinct intonation patterns and vocabulary influenced by the tribal communities in the region.

Bundeli is an Indo-Aryan language spoken in the Bundelkhand region, encompassing northern Madhya Pradesh and parts of Uttar Pradesh. It is considered an Apabhramsa (corrupted form) of Shauraseni Prakrit and was termed 'Bundeli' by George Grierson. Predominant in districts like Tikamgarh, Niwari, Sagar, Panna, Damoh, Chhatarpur, and Narsinghpur, Bundeli reflects the rich cultural heritage of the region.

Bagheli, an Eastern Hindi language, is prevalent in the Baghelkhand region, covering districts such as Rewa, Satna, Singrauli, Shahdol, Umaria, and Sidhi in Madhya Pradesh. Halam is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Halam community in Tripura. It comprises various sub-dialects, reflecting the diversity within the Halam tribe.

Garo is a Tibeto-Burman language spoken by the Garo tribe in Tripura. It has multiple dialects and is also spoken in Meghalaya and neighboring regions.
An Indo-Aryan language, Bishnupriya Manipuri is spoken by a section of the Manipuri community in Tripura. It incorporates elements from Sanskrit, Bengali, and Meitei.
A Sino-Tibetan language, Manipuri is spoken by the Meitei community in Tripura. It is also the official language of the neighboring state of Manipur.
A cluster of Tibeto-Burman languages spoken by Kuki and Mizo communities in Tripura. These languages exhibit mutual intelligibility and share cultural ties.
Reang, also known as Bru, is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Reang tribe in Tripura. It is considered endangered due to declining numbers of speakers.

Garhwali is an Indo-Aryan language spoken predominantly in the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand, encompassing districts like Pauri Garhwal, Tehri Garhwal, and Uttarkashi. Kumaoni is an Indo-Aryan language spoken in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand, covering districts such as Almora, Nainital, and Pithoragarh. The language boasts various dialects, including Central Kumaoni, Eastern Kumaoni, and Western Kumaoni, each exhibiting distinct linguistic features.

Jaunsari is spoken by the Jaunsari tribal community in the Jaunsar-Bawar region of Dehradun district. While often considered a dialect of Garhwali, Jaunsari possesses unique linguistic characteristics that set it apart. UNESCO has classified Jaunsari as a 'definitely endangered' language.
Rangkas is a Sino-Tibetan language once spoken by the Rangkas community in the Pithoragarh district. The language is now considered extinct, with no known speakers remaining.

Byangsi is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Byangsi community in the Byans Valley of Pithoragarh district. It is one of the lesser-known languages of Uttarakhand, reflecting the rich linguistic diversity of the region.
Chaudangsi is spoken by the Chaudangsi community in the Darma Valley of Pithoragarh district. This Sino-Tibetan language is closely related to Byangsi and shares several linguistic features.
Darmiya is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken in the Darma Valley of Pithoragarh district. It is one of the lesser-known languages of Uttarakhand, contributing to the state's rich linguistic tapestry.
Raji is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Raji tribal community in the Pithoragarh and Champawat districts. The language is considered endangered, with a declining number of speakers.
Rawat is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Rawat community in the Bageshwar and Pithoragarh districts. It is among the lesser-documented languages of Uttarakhand.

Jad is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Jad community in the Uttarkashi district. The language is part of the broader Tibeto-Burman language family and reflects the cultural heritage of the Jad people.
Rongpo is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Rongpo community in the Chamoli district. It contributes to the linguistic diversity of Uttarakhand's Himalayan region.
Buksa is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by the Buksa tribal community in the Udham Singh Nagar district. It is one of the minority languages of Uttarakhand, reflecting the state's cultural diversity.

Tharu is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by the Tharu community in the southern plains of Uttarakhand, particularly in the Udham Singh Nagar district. The language has several dialects and is also spoken in neighboring Nepal.

Doteli is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by a segment of the population in the eastern regions of Uttarakhand, particularly in areas bordering Nepal. It shares linguistic similarities with Kumaoni and Nepali.
Mahasu Pahari is an Indo-Aryan language spoken in the western parts of Uttarakhand, especially in the Uttarkashi district. It is closely related to other Pahari languages of the region.

Awadhi is an Indo-Aryan dialect spoken in the Awadh region of Uttar Pradesh, encompassing districts such as Lucknow, Faizabad, and Barabanki. Braj Bhasha is spoken in the Braj region, including Mathura, Agra, and Aligarh districts. Known for its association with the poetry of Surdas and its use in devotional songs dedicated to Lord Krishna, Braj Bhasha holds significant cultural importance in Uttar Pradesh.

Bundeli is spoken in the Bundelkhand region, covering districts like Jhansi, Mahoba, and Banda. It is closely related to Braj Bhasha and has its own distinct linguistic features, contributing to the cultural diversity of Uttar Pradesh.

Bhojpuri is an Eastern Indo-Aryan language spoken in the Purvanchal region of Uttar Pradesh, including districts such as Varanasi, Gorakhpur, and Azamgarh. It has a vibrant oral tradition and is also spoken in parts of Bihar and Jharkhand.

Khariboli, also known as Kauravi, is spoken in the western districts of Uttar Pradesh, including Meerut and Saharanpur. It forms the basis of Standard Hindi and has played a crucial role in the development of modern Hindi literature.

Urdu is widely spoken in Uttar Pradesh, particularly in cities like Lucknow and Aligarh. It has a rich literary heritage and has been used extensively in poetry and prose, reflecting the cultural amalgamation of the region.

Tharu is a language spoken by the Tharu tribal community in the Terai region of Uttar Pradesh, especially in districts like Lakhimpur Kheri and Bahraich. It belongs to the Indo-Aryan language family and reflects the unique cultural heritage of the Tharu people.

Bhoksa is a lesser-known language spoken by the Bhoksa tribal community in parts of Uttar Pradesh. It is considered endangered, with a declining number of speakers, and efforts are being made to document and preserve this unique dialect.

Bengali is the official and most widely spoken language in West Bengal, belonging to the Indo-Aryan language family. It has a rich literary tradition and serves as a unifying medium among various communities in the state.

Mundari is an Austroasiatic language spoken by the Munda tribe in parts of West Bengal, especially in the districts of Purulia and Paschim Medinipur. It has a rich oral tradition and is integral to the cultural identity of the Munda people.
Lepcha is a Sino-Tibetan language spoken by the Lepcha community in the Darjeeling district of West Bengal. It has its own script and is known for its unique phonological features.

Chakma is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by the Chakma community in parts of West Bengal. It has its own script and shares linguistic features with Bengali and Assamese.

Zangskari is a dialect of Ladakhi spoken in the Zanskar region. It has four sub-dialects: Stod, Zhung, Sham, and Lungna. Zangskari reflects the unique cultural and linguistic heritage of the Zanskar valley.
The Changthang dialect is spoken by the Changpa nomads in the Changtang region of eastern Ladakh. This dialect reflects the nomadic lifestyle and high-altitude pastoral culture of the Changpa people.

Etikoppaka toys are wooden lacquerware toys crafted in the Etikoppaka village of Andhra Pradesh. Made from softwood called Ankudu, these toys are colored with natural dyes and known for their smooth finish and vibrant hues.
Kondapalli toys are handcrafted wooden figurines from Kondapalli village near Vijayawada. Made from Tella Poniki wood, these toys often depict scenes from rural life, deities, and animals.

Durgi stone craft originates from Durgi village in Andhra Pradesh, where artisans carve intricate idols and sculptures from locally available soft limestone. It is widely used in temple architecture and decorative pieces.

Tholu Bommalata is the traditional shadow puppetry art of Andhra Pradesh. Artisans create large, colorful leather puppets depicting characters from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, which are used in storytelling performances.

Budithi brassware hails from the village of Budithi in Srikakulam district. This metal craft features elegant brass and bell metal artifacts, utensils, and decorative items, often with geometric designs.

Bidriware is a unique metal handicraft with Persian influences, featuring intricate silver inlay work on blackened metal. Though more popular in Karnataka, Bidri art is also practiced in Andhra Pradesh.
Wooden lacquerware is a traditional craft where artisans coat wooden objects with vibrant lacquered designs. The craft is prominent in various parts of Andhra Pradesh, particularly in Etikoppaka.

Butta Bommalu, meaning 'basket dolls,' are traditional bobblehead dolls made from lightweight materials like papier-mâché and wood. These dolls are characterized by their oversized heads and bright colors, representing deities and cultural figures.

Tikuli is a traditional art form from Bihar that involves the creation of intricate designs on glass, adorned with gold and silver foils. Today, Tikuli art has evolved to include decorative items and paintings, reflecting the rich cultural heritage of the region.

It is an offshoot of Mughal miniature painting, characterized by its focus on daily life, local festivals, and bazaar scenes. Unlike Mughal paintings, Patna Kalam emphasizes simplicity and lacks elaborate backgrounds.

Bihar has a rich tradition of stone and terracotta sculpture dating back to ancient times. The region is renowned for its intricate stone carvings and terracotta figures, which often depict deities, mythological scenes, and aspects of daily life. Wood carving is a traditional craft in Bihar, where artisans skillfully carve intricate designs into wooden objects. This art form is evident in various items, including furniture, decorative panels, and religious idols, showcasing the state's rich cultural heritage.

Artisans, particularly from tribal communities, create a range of products such as baskets, mats, and furniture using locally sourced bamboo and cane. Dhokra is an ancient metal casting technique practiced by the Ghadwas of Bastar and the Jharas of Raigarh in Chhattisgarh. Utilizing the lost-wax method, artisans create intricate bell metal figurines, often depicting tribal deities, animals, and cultural motifs.

Terracotta art in Chhattisgarh involves crafting figures from locally sourced clay. Artisans mold and fire the clay to produce items such as elephants, horses, and ritualistic objects, reflecting the state's rich cultural heritage.

Bastar region is renowned for its woodcraft, where artisans carve intricate designs into teak, Indian rosewood, and other local woods. The carvings often depict scenes from tribal life, animals, and deities, showcasing the region's artistic traditions.

Chhattisgarh's stone carving tradition features artisans sculpting intricate designs into sandstone and other locally available stones. The carvings include statues of deities, decorative panels, and architectural elements, reflecting the region's historical artistry.

Utilizing the abundant bamboo resources, artisans in Chhattisgarh create a variety of items such as baskets, mats, and decorative pieces. The craft showcases the community's resourcefulness and connection to their natural environment.

Inspired by traditional tattoo art, Godna paintings are created on paper and cloth using natural dyes. The motifs often include tribal symbols, animals, and daily activities, reflecting the cultural narratives of the region.

Practiced by the Rathwa and Bhilala tribes, Pithora paintings are ritualistic murals created on the walls of houses. They depict folklore, deities, and significant events, serving both decorative and ceremonial purposes.

Goa's wood carving tradition involves creating intricate designs on furniture, altars, and religious artifacts, reflecting a blend of Indian and Portuguese aesthetics. Artisans craft detailed floral patterns, figures of saints, and other motifs, showcasing exceptional craftsmanship.

Goan potters create functional and decorative items, including garden pots, bowls with floral designs, and figures of saints. These crafts are deeply rooted in Goan culture and are appreciated by visitors for their rustic charm.

Bidriware is a traditional metal handicraft from Telangana, involving the inlaying of silver or gold into blackened alloy. The intricate designs often feature floral and geometric patterns, reflecting the region's rich artistic heritage.

Pochampally Ikat weaving is a traditional textile art from Telangana, known for its distinctive tie-and-dye technique. The weavers create intricate patterns on silk and cotton fabrics, producing sarees and other textiles.

Telia Rumal is a traditional handloom craft from Telangana, where artisans use a unique oil-dyeing technique to create vibrant patterns on cotton fabrics. The process involves dyeing the yarns in oil and natural dyes before weaving them into intricate designs.

Gollabhama art is a traditional folk art from Telangana, depicting scenes of rural life, especially those related to cattle herding. The paintings are characterized by simple lines and vibrant colors, reflecting the pastoral lifestyle of the region.

Tripura is renowned for its bamboo and cane crafts, with artisans creating a variety of items such as baskets, mats, furniture, and decorative pieces. These crafts reflect the ingenuity of the indigenous communities and their harmonious relationship with nature.

Wood carving in Tripura involves the creation of intricate designs on wooden surfaces, including furniture, utensils, and decorative items. This craft showcases the artistic skills of the artisans and is deeply rooted in the state's cultural heritage.

Pottery in Tripura involves the crafting of earthenware items such as pots, figurines, and decorative pieces. The craft reflects the utilitarian and artistic sensibilities of the indigenous communities.

Bamboo root carving is an intricate art form that involves transforming the naturally shaped roots of bamboo plants into detailed sculptures and decorative items. This craft highlights the creativity and skill of the artisans.
Stone carving in Tripura includes the creation of sculptures and decorative items from stone, reflecting the rich cultural heritage and artistic traditions of the region.

Likhai is a traditional wood carving art form practiced in Uttarakhand, particularly in the Kumaon region. Ringal bamboo crafts involve weaving and crafting items from the locally available ringal bamboo. Artisans create baskets, mats, and other household items using traditional techniques, showcasing the sustainable use of natural resources and the ingenuity of rural communities in Uttarakhand.

Aipan is a traditional folk art of Uttarakhand, primarily practiced by women. It involves creating geometric and floral patterns on the floors and walls of homes during festivals and special occasions. The art is done using a paste made from rice flour and is believed to bring prosperity and ward off evil spirits.

Copper craft in Uttarakhand includes the creation of utensils, decorative items, and jewelry using copper. Artisans employ traditional techniques to craft items like pots, pans, and ornaments, reflecting the region's metalworking heritage and the practical use of locally sourced materials.

Dokra metal craft is an ancient technique of metal casting practiced by tribal communities in Uttarakhand. Artisans use the lost-wax method to create intricate metal sculptures, often depicting animals, deities, and tribal motifs. Chikankari is a traditional hand-embroidery technique from Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, characterized by delicate patterns on fabrics like chiffon, muslin, organza, and silk. Zardozi is a traditional form of heavy and elaborate metal embroidery from Uttar Pradesh, involving the use of gold and silver threads to create intricate patterns. This technique is applied to decorative items like wall hangings, cushion covers, and upholstery, reflecting the opulence of Mughal art.

Khurja pottery, originating from the town of Khurja in Uttar Pradesh, is renowned for its glazed ceramic ware. Artisans produce a variety of items, including decorative vases, plates, and tiles, featuring vibrant colors and intricate designs, often inspired by Mughal and Persian art.

Moradabad, known as the 'Brass City,' is famous for its metal crafts, particularly brassware. Artisans create decorative items such as vases, trays, and sculptures, showcasing intricate designs and high-quality craftsmanship, reflecting the region's rich metalworking tradition.

Saharanpur in Uttar Pradesh is renowned for its wood carving industry. Artisans craft decorative items like furniture, panels, and artifacts, featuring intricate floral and geometric patterns, reflecting the region's rich cultural heritage.

Bhadohi, known as the 'Carpet City,' is famous for its hand-knotted carpets. Artisans create intricate designs on carpets, often inspired by Mughal art, showcasing the region's rich weaving tradition.

Chowk Poorana is a traditional floor art practiced in Uttar Pradesh, where women draw intricate designs on the floor using rice flour and colored powders during festivals and auspicious occasions. These designs often feature geometric patterns and motifs inspired by local folklore.

Terracotta art in West Bengal includes the creation of idols, decorative items, and architectural elements. The terracotta temples of Bishnupur, adorned with intricate reliefs, are prime examples of this craft.

Constructed in the 12th century by the Kakatiya dynasty, this temple is dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu, and Surya. It features intricately carved pillars and star-shaped shrines, reflecting Kakatiya architecture.
The second longest cave system in India, known for its stalactite and stalagmite formations. Historically, it served as a meditation site for Buddhist monks.
An ancient Buddhist monument dating back to the 2nd century BCE, renowned for its grand architecture and intricate carvings depicting Buddhist teachings.
A 11th-century temple dedicated to Lord Narasimha, showcasing a blend of Kalinga and Chalukya architectural styles. It's known for its stone carvings and the annual Chandanotsavam festival.

Perched atop Indrakeeladri hill, this temple is dedicated to Goddess Kanaka Durga. It exhibits Dravidian architectural style and is a significant pilgrimage site, especially during the Dasara festival.

A complex of nine temples dedicated to Lord Narasimha, located in the Nallamala hills. The architecture ranges from simple cave shrines to grand Dravidian structures, reflecting various dynastic influences.
One of the Pancharama Kshetras, this temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and showcases exquisite stone carvings and a towering gopuram, exemplifying Dravidian architecture.
Known as the 'Grand Canyon of India,' this fort overlooks the Pennar River and features medieval fortifications, temples, and a mosque, reflecting a blend of Hindu and Islamic architectural styles.
One of the most visited pilgrimage sites globally, this temple is dedicated to Lord Venkateswara. It showcases Dravidian architecture with a towering gopuram and intricate carvings.
Also known as the Godavari Bridge, it's one of the longest road-cum-rail bridges in Asia, exemplifying modern engineering marvels in the state.
A hill fort built during the Vijayanagara Empire, known for its strategic location, fortifications, and remnants of ancient structures, reflecting military architecture of the period.
A temple dedicated to Lord Satyanarayana, known for its unique chariot-like structure and panoramic views of the surrounding region.

Founded in the 17th century, Tawang Monastery is the largest monastery in India and the second largest in the world. It is a significant center for Mahayana Buddhism and showcases traditional Buddhist architectural styles.
A historical fort located in the West Kameng district, Dirang Dzong reflects the traditional fortified architecture of the Monpa tribe, constructed using stone and wood.

Dating back to the 8th century, Bhismaknagar Fort is an archaeological site near Roing. Built with fired bricks, it is associated with the Chutia kingdom and showcases early medieval fort architecture.
An archaeological site containing the ruins of a 13th-14th century temple near Likabali. The temple features intricate stone sculptures and is linked to the Chutia dynasty.
Located in Itanagar, Ita Fort dates back to the 14th-15th century. Built with bricks, the fort has three entrances and is believed to have been constructed by the Chutia kings.
The Apatani tribe constructs stilt houses using bamboo and wood. These elevated structures protect against floods and pests, reflecting the tribe's adaptation to their environment.

The Wancho tribe in Longding district builds houses using locally sourced materials like wood, bamboo, and palm leaves. These structures are elevated and feature thatched roofs, showcasing indigenous building techniques.
The Monpa tribe constructs houses using materials such as earth, stone, timber, and bamboo. Their architecture harmonizes with the natural environment and reflects sustainable building practices.
Designed by STUDIOARO, the Great Hornbill Gate serves as the iconic entry to the Donyi Polo Airport. It blends traditional bamboo construction with modern design elements.

Also known as Kechai-Khati Temple, this ancient temple near Sadiya was dedicated to a primordial female tribal deity. Built without mortar, the temple featured intricate stone carvings and a copper-sheeted roof.

An 18th-century two-storied pavilion in Sivasagar, built by Ahom king Pramatta Singha. It served as a royal sports pavilion for Ahom kings and nobles to watch traditional games like buffalo fights, especially during the Rongali Bihu festival. The structure is renowned for its unique Ahom architecture, featuring an inverted boat-shaped roof and arched entrances.

Located in Rangpur, near Sivasagar, this 18th-century palace and military base was constructed by Ahom king Rajeswar Singha. Originally serving as an army base, it comprises seven stories, including three underground levels (now sealed) and two secret tunnels. The structure showcases a blend of indigenous architectural styles and materials.

Situated in Garhgaon, near Sivasagar, this palace was the royal residence of the Ahom kings. Initially built in 1752 by King Rudra Singha, it underwent several renovations. The multi-storied structure exemplifies Ahom architecture, with its grand halls, chambers, and intricately designed facades.

A group of three Hindu temples—Sivadol, Vishnudol, and Devidol—located on the banks of the Sivasagar tank. Built by Queen Ambika, wife of Ahom king Swargadeo Siba Singha, in 1734, these temples are dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu, and Durga, respectively. Sivadol, the tallest among them, stands at about 104 feet and is a prime example of the Nilachal architectural style.

Located in Jorhat, this palace was the residence of the last Ahom king, Purandar Singha. The structure reflects traditional Ahom architectural elements and offers insights into the region's royal heritage.

Often referred to as the 'Pyramids of Assam,' these are burial mounds of Ahom kings and nobles located in Charaideo. Established by the first Ahom king, Sukaphaa, in the 13th century, the maidams are revered for their archaeological and spiritual significance, showcasing a unique blend of Hindu and tribal burial practices.

Established in 1876 by D. Slimmon, the club boasts the world's third-oldest golf course and the oldest in Asia. The colonial-era architecture includes a clubhouse, polo ground, and cricket field, reflecting British colonial influences in Assam.

Founded by Vaishnavite saint Madhavdeva in 1583, this satra (monastic institution) in Barpeta is a significant center for Assamese art, culture, and spirituality. The complex includes prayer halls, monks' quarters, and traditional Assamese architectural features.

Perched on the Nilachal Hill in Guwahati, this ancient temple is dedicated to the goddess Kamakhya. It's one of the oldest of the 51 Shakti Pithas and is renowned for its unique architectural style, featuring a beehive-like shikhara and sculpted panels depicting Hindu deities.

Located in Hajo, this mosque is believed to have been built by Pir Giasuddin Auliya and is said to contain soil brought from Mecca. The structure reflects medieval Islamic architecture and holds significant religious importance for Assamese Muslims.

An architectural marvel from the Ahom era, this stone bridge was constructed over the Namdang River in 1703 during the reign of Swargadeo Rudra Singha. Carved out of a single solid rock, it exemplifies the engineering prowess of the time and remains in use today.
